name: Structure and goal pursuit
statement: Reminders that the world runs on orderly patterns rather than randomness are held to raise willingness to work towards unrelated personal goals.
meaning: The claim comes in a narrow form and a broad one. The narrow form is experimental. Show someone a passage, a word task or a questionnaire that presents the world as patterned, and they report more willingness to spend effort on a goal that has nothing to do with the passage. The broad form is dispositional. People who believe their actions reliably produce outcomes are said to pursue goals harder than people who do not. Only the narrow form has been tested at scale, and the verdict below is about that form alone. The reasoning behind both is the same. Effort is a bet on a link between what a person does and what happens next, and a world with no reliable patterns pays nothing on that bet. The idea sits inside compensatory control theory, whose better-known claim runs the other way: that threats to personal control push people towards order-providing beliefs. That second claim is separate and is not assessed here. Just-world belief and system justification are neighbours in the same tradition, and both have their own entries.

origin.who: Aaron C. Kay, Kristin Laurin, Gráinne M. Fitzsimons and Mark J. Landau
origin.note: The paper is a brief report, "A functional basis for structure-seeking: Exposure to structure promotes willingness to engage in motivated action", published online first on 23 September 2013 and in the February 2014 issue. Its authors describe it as the first test of an assumption they trace to Lerner's just-world theory, to Heine, Proulx and Vohs's meaning maintenance model, and to their own 2008 compensatory control work. Three different manipulations run across its five studies, and the phrase "exposure to structure" covers all three.

evidence: Five experiments used undergraduates or American workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk, and three separate manipulations. Studies 1 to 3 had people read a short article about how trees grow leaves, framed either as an orderly pattern or as natural randomness. In Study 1, 103 undergraduates rated willingness to work and make sacrifices for four assigned long-term goals. The structure condition averaged 5.65 against 5.16 for the random condition, t(67) = 2.33, p < .03, Cohen's d = 0.57, with a neutral condition at 5.45 in between and different from neither. Study 2 ran the same articles on 67 online participants using goals they named themselves, and got 5.26 against 4.72, t(65) = 2.00, p = .05, d = 0.50. Study 3 repeated Study 2 on 66 people and added timing measures. Its motivation index came to 5.59 against 4.88, t(62) = 2.13, p = .04, d = 0.55, planned time on a rating scale to 5.30 against 4.38, t(64) = 2.36, p = .02, d = 0.60, and planned minutes to 1,721 against 792, t(64) = 2.36, p = .02, d = 0.60. Study 4 swapped the article for a scrambled-sentence task built from structure words or randomness words, then told 67 people to stop and spend a minute doing something towards a goal they had listed. Of those primed with structure 94% reported acting, against 76% primed with randomness, chi-square(1, N = 67) = 4.02, p < .05. Study 5 dropped the randomness condition for a baseline and induced structure by asking people to rate how patterned ten world events are, five of them chosen as orderly. Of 132 participants, 83% in the order condition acted against 65% at baseline, chi-square(1, N = 132) = 5.70, p < .02. Study 5 also measured generalised contingency belief with two items and found the effect only among people low on it, B = 1.86, Wald = 8.52, p = .004, and absent among people high on it, B = -0.03, Wald = 0.003, p = .96.

replication.headline: Many Labs 2 repeated Study 2 in 6,506 people and got d = -0.02, with not one sample in the project returning a significant difference in either direction.
replication.detail: The replication is multi-laboratory, not one team's attempt. Many Labs 2 followed the Registered Report model, had its materials and protocol peer reviewed before data collection, and preregistered the accepted design at the Open Science Framework. It tested 28 findings across about 125 samples and 15,305 participants from 36 countries and territories, split into two half-hour slates. Structure and goal pursuit sat in Slate 1, and the version chosen was Study 2, the tree articles with self-nominated goals. Participants who read the structured article scored 5.48 against 5.51 for the random article, t(6,498.63) = -0.94, p = 0.35, d = -0.02, 95% CI [-0.07, 0.03], on N = 6,506. The median effect across samples was also -0.02. Table 2 records 0.00% of samples significant in the original direction, 0.00% significant in the opposite direction, and 100.00% not significant. Heterogeneity was absent, Q = 33.95, df = 51, p = 0.97, I-squared = 0%, 95% CI [0%, 2%]. Splitting WEIRD from less WEIRD samples gave Q = 3.10, p = 0.08, and laboratory against online gave Q = 2.06, p = 0.15. Position in the slate made no difference: d = -0.01, 95% CI [-0.18, 0.17] when the task came first, d = 0.10, 95% CI [-0.08, 0.27] when it came last. Table 5 records the replication test at p = 0.347. Three figures for the original circulate and they do not agree. Table 2 gives d = 0.49, 95% CI [0.001, 0.973], the project's own finding report for this effect prints the upper bound as 0.980, and the original paper prints d = 0.50 with no interval at all.

study.cite: Klein, R. A., Vianello, M., Hasselman, F., et al. (2018). Many Labs 2: Investigating variation in replicability across samples and settings. Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(4), 443-490.

replicated.weighting: global effect size pooling all samples in the slate

limits: The replication covers one of the five original studies. Studies 1, 4 and 5 used other manipulations and other outcome measures, and no repeat of them at comparable scale turned up in Crossref, in Semantic Scholar's list of the 104 papers citing the original, or in Europe PMC. The original authors' own Study 5 predicts a flat average. The effect there appeared only among people who did not already believe their actions produce outcomes, and vanished among people who did. Laurin, Kay and Landau pressed that argument in a commentary in the same issue as Many Labs 2. They accept that the project failed to reproduce the finding, allow that their results may have been artefacts, and report an exploratory test using the project's single-item self-esteem measure as a stand-in for the moderator, run on United States and Canadian data from the third of the sample released first. Only the opening page of that commentary was obtained, from the full-text extract stored at Semantic Scholar, because Sage returns 403 to automated requests. The result of their exploratory test is therefore not quoted here. They also point to Khenfer, Roux, Tafani and Laurin, who report that reminders of a powerful God raised goal commitment only among people low in self-efficacy. That paper was named but not retrieved. Schimmelpfennig and colleagues re-examined Many Labs 2's cultural comparisons and found the design underpowered for detecting heterogeneity between WEIRD and less WEIRD samples, which bears on how much the flat cross-country picture can settle. For this effect, every heterogeneity estimate the project reported was zero.
misreadings: The tested claim is about a momentary prime, not about a trait. Believing the world is orderly and being made to think about order for two minutes are different things, and Many Labs 2 speaks only to the second. Nothing in it tests whether people who chronically perceive structure pursue goals harder. Kay and colleagues found that pattern in Study 5's baseline condition, where contingency belief predicted goal pursuit at B = 0.83, Wald = 6.17, p < .02. The second error is to read the null as a verdict on compensatory control theory. The programme's central claim points the other way, that threats to control drive people towards order-providing beliefs, and the 2014 paper cites Whitson and Galinsky's pattern-perception result as its starting point rather than testing it. The just-world and system-justification literatures are cousins with their own replication records, and this result neither supports nor damages them. Counting the original as five independent successes also overstates it. The authors call Study 3 an exact and conceptual replication of Study 2, and their own footnote reports that dropping the goal-value covariate raises Study 3's p to .106.
